overview:
It began in March 2011 with graffiti in the southern town of Daraa — schoolboys writing an Arab Spring slogan about the fall of the regime — and with the torture of the children who wrote it. Protests spread through Homs, Hama, Damascus and the Aleppo countryside. Where other governments that year offered concessions or collapsed, Bashar al-Assad answered with live fire, mass detention, and by the winter of 2011 with tanks and artillery against his own cities; the siege of Homs that began that year set the template for everything after. Army defectors and neighborhood militias coalesced loosely as the Free Syrian Army, a political opposition-in-exile formed abroad, and neither ever really cohered. By 2012 the fighting was a full war, with the battle of Aleppo splitting Syria's largest city along a front line that would hold for four years, and massacres such as Houla marking how far the violence against civilians had already gone.

What made the war so long was that almost no one fighting it was fighting alone. Iran and Hezbollah kept the government's manpower from running out; Gulf states, Turkey and Western intelligence services armed and quarrelled over a fractured opposition. Jihadist factions grew out of the vacuum, and the Islamic State, expanding from Iraq in 2013–14, seized Raqqa and much of the east — which in turn drew in a US-led air coalition and made Syria's Kurds, who held the northeast, into Washington's ground partner after they broke the siege of Kobanî in early 2015. Government forces used chemical weapons repeatedly; the sarin attack on Ghouta in August 2013 killed around 1,400 people and produced not the promised Western strike but a deal to dismantle the declared arsenal, after which barrel bombs, starvation sieges and further chemical attacks continued. Russia's air campaign from September 2015 reversed the regime's decline and, with it, took Aleppo in December 2016. Turkey meanwhile launched its own incursions — Euphrates Shield, then later operations — aimed as much at containing Kurdish autonomy as at ISIS. The United States struck Syrian government targets directly at Shayrat in 2017, and Turkish and Russian aircraft had already clashed over the border in 2015; the war had become a place where great powers tested each other at close range.

By around 2019 the map had largely frozen: the government held the west with Russian and Iranian backing, Kurdish-led forces the northeast, Turkey a strip of the north, and a rebel and jihadist enclave survived in Idlib under a shaky ceasefire while an earthquake, economic collapse and the drug trade in captagon ground on. Then in late 2024 the props gave way — Hezbollah battered by Israel, Iran weakened, Russia absorbed in Ukraine — and an offensive led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham took Aleppo, Hama and Homs in under two weeks. Damascus fell on 8 December 2024 and Assad fled to Moscow, ending fifty-four years of family rule. Estimates of the dead range from the UN's minimum of about 350,000 individually identified through 2021 to well over 600,000 counted by the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights; more than a hundred thousand people were forcibly disappeared, and roughly half the prewar population — some fourteen million — was driven from home.
significance: More than any other conflict of its era, this one defined what the post-2011 world would tolerate. The failure to enforce the "red line" after Ghouta, the survival of a government that besieged and gassed its own cities, and the return of Russian military power to the Middle East together reset the expectations of governments everywhere about the cost of mass atrocity. It produced the largest displacement crisis since the Second World War, and the arrival of Syrians in Turkey, Lebanon, Jordan and Europe reshaped European politics and border policy for a decade. It gave the Islamic State the territory from which it projected a global campaign, and it gave Syria's Kurds a self-governing region whose fate is still unsettled. That Assad's rule ended not through negotiation or intervention but through the sudden exhaustion of his foreign patrons is its own lesson about how durable-looking regimes actually fall.
coverage: Written from the CFR conflict backgrounder, Britannica and Wikipedia's war and casualties articles, plus UNHCR's regional data portal; the dataset's 114 events cluster heavily in 2011–2017 and the notable sample includes nothing after 2017, so the frozen-front years, Idlib, and the 2024 collapse are thinner on the map than in this text. The underlying record is genuinely contested rather than merely incomplete: casualty counts differ by more than 300,000 between monitors using inconsistent definitions of who counts as a civilian, deaths inside government-held areas were systematically hard to document, the fate of the disappeared is largely unknown pending work in the prisons and mass graves opened after December 2024, and much reporting on all sides came from parties with a stake in the outcome.
